title: Each Term Sums the Two Before
statement:
A sequence starts with F(0) = 0 and F(1) = 1. Every later term is the sum of the two terms right before it: F(k) = F(k − 1) + F(k − 2) for k ≥ 2.

Given n, return F(n).

examples.why: The sequence goes 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8. Counting starts at index 0.
F(1) is one of the two given starting values.
The very first term is 0, not 1.

hints: The definition is already a recursive function. Write it, then count how often it computes F(2) for n = 6.
Every term depends only on the two terms before it. Do you need the rest of the sequence?
Walk forward from (0, 1) and keep only the last two values, replacing them with (b, a + b) at each step.

explain.intuition:
Translating the definition straight into recursion works but is very slow: F(n) calls F(n − 1) and F(n − 2), and both of those repeat the same work again. The call tree roughly doubles at each level, so the cost grows like 1.6n.

The fix is the core idea of dynamic programming: solve each smaller case once. Build the sequence from the bottom, and since each term only needs the previous two, keep just two variables. It is like memoising a selector: same input, compute once.
pitfalls: Starting the sequence at 1, 1 so every answer is shifted by one index. Here F(0) = 0.
Running the loop one time too many or too few. Check it by hand on n = 2 (answer 1) and n = 3 (answer 2).
Shipping the plain recursion. It is fine for n = 30, but it is exponential; any larger limit breaks it.

solutions.title: Recursion straight from the definition
solutions.idea: Return n for n < 2, otherwise the sum of the two recursive calls. It repeats the same subproblems over and over.

solutions.title: Bottom-up with two variables
solutions.idea: Walk forward from F(0) and F(1), keeping only the last two terms.

solutions.title: Fast doubling
solutions.idea: From F(k) and F(k+1) you can get F(2k) and F(2k+1) directly: F(2k) = F(k)·(2F(k+1) − F(k)) and F(2k+1) = F(k)² + F(k+1)². Halving n each step gives logarithmic time.

followups: n can now be up to 10¹⁸ and you return the answer modulo 1 000 000 007. Which solution still works?
Add a cache to the recursive version. What do its time and space become?
